bridge: Builds on O02: assets, threats and authorised scope. Use fictional account details; never put recovery codes in this notebook.
teaching:
An account connects an identity to capabilities. A password is one authentication factor; a second independent factor reduces dependence on that password. A passkey can also resist common phishing flows by binding authentication to a site. Recovery is part of authentication: a weak recovery email can bypass a strong primary login.

Start with an inventory: service, importance, recovery route, multi-factor status and last backup test. Record status, not secret values. Prioritise email and the password manager because they often unlock other accounts. Update devices, lock screens and restrict extensions because account security also depends on the endpoint that handles the session.

A backup should survive the failure you care about. A file copied to the same disk helps with accidental editing but not disk loss. Synchronisation may replicate a deletion, so it is not automatically a historical backup. Choose a retention period, keep an independent recovery copy and restore a harmless file to verify your process. Privacy adds a separate question: even if a service protects data, does it need to collect that data at all?
example:
Fictional inventory
Service        Importance   MFA       Recovery     Restore test
Demo email     high         enabled   offline kit  not applicable
Local notebook medium       device    spare copy   2026-10-29
Photo archive  medium       account   email        not tested

Do not include passwords, real recovery codes or session tokens.
explanation: The photo archive is marked not tested, so it is a recovery risk even if a backup tool reports success. The demo email has higher priority because it recovers the archive account. An offline recovery kit needs protected storage; the inventory should say where the process is documented without exposing the secret itself.
exercise: Using invented services, make three inventory rows. Copy a harmless note to a separate recovery location, remove only a disposable working copy, then restore it. Record original contents, restored contents and what failure your copy would not survive.
solution: The restored contents match. A same-disk copy does not survive disk failure. The inventory contains no authentication secrets. A good explanation links the recovery chain from one service to another.
challenge: A fictional laptop and its disk are lost. Email recovery codes existed only on that laptop; a cloud folder synchronised deletions. Identify two independent recovery weaknesses and propose a test for each.
challenge_solution: Use protected recovery material accessible without the lost laptop, and a versioned/independent backup whose retention survives deletion. Test sign-in recovery with a safe planned procedure and restore an invented file from a historical version; never disable your only working factor as a casual experiment.
